claims.text: HEAs consist of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The initial nanoparticles are single-phase FCC or BCC solid solutions with homogeneous elemental distributions.
Structural and chemical stability is governed by the interplay of configurational entropy and lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch.
High configurational entropy favors a mixed solid-solution structure at elevated temperature.
Large differences in constituent atomic sizes produce pronounced lattice distortion.
Pronounced lattice distortion reduces atomic diffusivity.
Reduced atomic diffusivity kinetically suppresses phase separation and chemical ordering.
Kinetic suppression of phase separation and ordering maintains structural and chemical integrity at high temperature.
Nanoparticles with greater lattice distortion will retain a single-phase XRD pattern and uniform EDX elemental distribution better than the low-distortion control.
Nanoparticles with greater lattice distortion will retain catalytic or thermoelectric performance better than the low-distortion control.
Nanoparticles with less lattice distortion may undergo phase segregation or chemical ordering.
Phase segregation or ordering will degrade functional properties relative to the as-synthesized state.
The proposed distortion-dependent stability relationship applies within the 473–1923 K operating range when kinetic barriers are not overcome.
Exposure far above 1923 K or for very prolonged durations may overcome the proposed kinetic stabilization.
Controlled inert or catalytic environments and constant pressure will limit oxidation and other extrinsic side reactions.
The magnitude of lattice distortion required to suppress diffusion is not known.
Local catalytic environments may influence nanoparticle stability independently of lattice distortion.
